title: Evaluating LLMs as a Bridge Between Cyber Threats and Business Risk for Executive Decision-Making
abstract: Security leaders cannot act on intelligence they cannot understand, yet most cyber threat intelligence (CTI) reporting is written for analysts, not executives. Bridging that gap manually is time-intensive, inconsistent, and difficult to scale for small CTI teams operating under resource constraints. Cloud-based AI writing tools supply one way forward but introduce data-exfiltration risks that security-sensitive organizations cannot accept, and ad hoc prompting without a formal evaluation framework produces outputs of unknown and unverifiable quality. This paper presents an evaluation of a locally deployable open-weight large language model tested across five prompt strategies of increasing sophistication against a corpus of real-world cyber incident reports, scored against a structured rubric by both an AI instrument and an independent human analyst. The findings show that prompt architecture, not model capability, is the primary driver of output quality, that the best-performing configuration produces executive-ready drafts at a fraction of the time required for manual authorship, and that AI-instrument scoring alone overestimates quality in a meaningful proportion of cases, underscoring the necessity of human review. CTI practitioners and security leaders will find in this paper a reproducible, on-premises framework for AI-assisted executive reporting with guidance on where current models succeed, where they fall short, and what prompt design choices make the difference.
domain: Cyber Threat Intelligence / Applied Natural Language Processing
problem_statement: CTI reporting is written in technical terms for analysts rather than executive decision-makers, creating a communication barrier. Cloud AI introduces data exfiltration risks, and ad hoc prompting yields unverifiable quality.
motivation: Enabling resource-constrained, security-sensitive CTI teams to reliably and safely generate executive-level business risk assessments on-premises without cloud exfiltration or enterprise-scale GPU infrastructure.
objectives: Evaluate whether a locally hosted large language model can convert technical cyber threat intelligence into executive-ready business risk summaries.
Identify what prompt conditions allow an LLM to reliably produce passing executive reports.
Compare AI-instrument scoring against human-analyst review to assess evaluation reliability.
research_questions: The study considers the extent to which AI-powered natural language processing can reduce the time required to translate technical cyber threat intelligence into business risk assessments that enable informed executive decision-making.
methodology: Controlled comparative experimental design following a generate-then-score workflow. In the generation phase, 20 real-world CTI reports across four threat categories were run through Gemma3:27b across five prompt strategies (S0-S4) for 10 iterations each (1,000 total summaries) using AnythingLLM with nomic-embed-text-v1 embeddings. In the scoring phase, reports were evaluated on a weighted four-dimension rubric (Actionability 35%, Analytical Rigor 30%, Language Appropriateness 20%, Structural Compliance 15%) on a 1-5 scale with a pass threshold of >= 3.5. Primary scoring was done blindly by an AI instrument, and an inter-rater comparison was performed on a random sample of 60 reports against independent human analyst scoring.
dataset: 20 real-world cyber incident reports drawn from public security vendor publications across four financial-sector-relevant threat categories: ransomware (5), supply chain attack (5), zero-day and edge device exploitation (5), and business email compromise (5). Sourced as PDFs and converted to Markdown.
preprocessing: Source PDF reports were converted to Markdown to preserve structural elements such as headings and lists for retrieval chunking, and each report was ingested into its own workspace session in AnythingLLM using nomic-embed-text-v1 embeddings (8,192-token context window).
models: Claude Sonnet 4.6 (Anthropic, cited in Section 2.6 / Appendix / References)

variables.name: Composite
variables.description: Weighted composite score summing four rubric dimensions

variables.name: Actionability
variables.description: Does the report give executives specific, decision-ready guidance? Weighted at 35%.

variables.name: Analytical Rigor
variables.description: Is the threat accurately characterized, with appropriate detail on actor behavior, attack method, and organizational impact? Weighted at 30%.

variables.name: Language Appropriateness
variables.description: Is the report written in plain, non-technical language suitable for a non-security executive audience? Weighted at 20%.

variables.name: Structural Compliance
variables.description: Does the report follow the required format, including BLUF placement where applicable, and complete all required sections? Weighted at 15%.

experimental_setup: MacBook Pro running Ollama for local LLM inference using Gemma3:27b at temperature 0.3. AnythingLLM local interface used for RAG with nomic-embed-text-v1 embeddings (8,192 tokens context). 20 source reports loaded individually into isolated workspace sessions. 5 prompt strategies (S0-S4) x 10 iterations per report = 1,000 generated executive summaries. Primary evaluation scored blindly across all 1,000 reports, and a 60-report validation subset was dually evaluated by human analyst.
evaluation_metrics: Pass rate (percentage of reports with composite score >= 3.5)
Dimension scores (Actionability, Analytical Rigor, Language Appropriateness, Structural Compliance on 1 to 5 scale)
Verdict-flip rate (percentage of dual-scored reports where pass/fail status flipped between raters)
Mean composite delta and mean absolute composite delta (|H - G|)
results: Across 1,000 reports under AI-instrument scoring: overall pass rate was 38.8% with a mean composite of 3.43 (SD = 0.185). By strategy: S0 achieved 3.50 composite / 61.0% pass rate; S1 achieved 3.22 composite / 1.5% pass rate; S2 achieved 3.37 composite / 20.0% pass rate; S3 achieved 3.44 composite / 38.0% pass rate; S4 achieved 3.60 composite / 73.5% pass rate. Category pass rates averaged across strategies: Ransomware (43.6%), BEC (42.8%), Zero-Day/Edge Device (42.4%), Supply Chain (26.4%). Dual-scoring validation (N=60): 38.3% agreement rate, 61.7% verdict-flip rate, mean composite AI = 3.431, human = 3.294 (mean delta -0.137, mean absolute delta 0.517). Mean generation time was 17.76 seconds at 66.25 tokens/sec.
conclusions: Prompt architecture is the primary driver of output quality rather than model scale alone. Strategy S4 combining BLUF and section content specifications achieves the highest quality (73.5% AI pass rate) and offers over 99% drafting time savings. However, AI-instrument scoring systematically overestimates quality (especially Language Appropriateness), yielding a 61.7% verdict-flip rate against human expert scoring, demonstrating that human review is essential.
limitations: Does not account for variation in executive reporting cultures, organizational risk tolerance frameworks, or internal communication expectations.
Does not employ a human-authored control group.
Only evaluates a single LLM (Gemma3:27b) at a single parameter scale.
Single-report workspace sessions in RAG do not model multi-document intelligence synthesis.
AI scoring instrument overestimates report quality relative to human analyst assessment.
future_work: Full re-scoring of the 1,000-report dataset by at least two independent CTI-qualified evaluators with a 30-50 report calibration exercise.
Replication across other model families (such as 70-billion-parameter open-weight models).
Testing multi-document ingestion and synthesis RAG pipelines.
Multi-turn self-evaluation/revision prompting and adding structured organizational context blocks into prompts.
explicit_assumptions: Composite score >= 3.5 represents output that is sufficiently complete and well-calibrated for an analyst to finalize for executive distribution.
Human analyst time per report is estimated at 8.0 hours (range 4-12 hours) based on literature estimates.
Embedding context window of 8,192 tokens allowed each source report to be fully processed before summary generation.

missing_information.description: Chunk 25 states AI scoring was performed by Claude (Sonnet 4.6), while Section 3.5 (Chunk 42, 43, 44) and Appendix D label the AI scoring instrument as 'Gemma3'.
missing_information.why_needed: Reproducing the AI-instrument scoring requires knowing whether Claude Sonnet 4.6 or Gemma3 was used as the scoring instrument.
missing_information.search_intent: Clarify AI scoring instrument Claude Sonnet 4.6 vs Gemma3 in CTI-LLM-Research

missing_information.gap_type: Exact Rubric Scoring Prompt / Rubric Scale Anchors
missing_information.description: The exact prompt text used to instruct the AI instrument to assign 1 to 5 scores on each of the 4 dimensions is not fully printed in the text (only dimension descriptions in Appendix A are provided).
missing_information.why_needed: Needed for exact replication of AI instrument scoring behavior.

conflicts.description: In Chunk 25, the paper states: 'Reports were submitted to Claude (Sonnet 4.6) in randomized batches... For each report, Claude applied the rubric...'. However, in Chunk 42, Chunk 43 (Figure 3), Chunk 44 (Figure 4), and Chunk 86/87 (Tables D-3, D-4), the AI scoring instrument is explicitly identified as 'Gemma3' ('scored by the AI instrument (Gemma3) used in the primary analysis').

In Chunk 70, the prompt for Strategy 1 states 'FORMAT: Structure your response using exactly these five sections:', but then lists only four numbered sections (1. Executive Summary, 2. Potential Business Impact, 3. Affected Systems / Scope, 4. Recommended Actions). Similarly, Strategy 3 in Chunk 78 states 'Structure your response using exactly these five sections;' followed by four sections.

sufficiency_reason: The paper provides full prompt templates for all five strategies (S0-S4 in Appendix B), the complete 4-dimension scoring rubric with weights (Appendix A), detailed aggregate and strategy-level pass rates, and the 60-report inter-rater comparison statistics (verdict-flip rate 61.7%, delta statistics). However, reproducing the AI-instrument scoring is complicated by a direct conflict in the text: Chunk 25 states the AI scoring instrument was Claude Sonnet 4.6, whereas Section 3.5 and Tables D-3/D-4 explicitly identify the scoring instrument as Gemma3. The GitHub repository is referenced for raw tracking data.
